Airmanship – the display of common sense, good aviation practices and high standard, in the air.
What are some indicators of good airmanship?
Airspeed accuracy
Thorough lookouts
Clear and accurate radio calls
Consideration for passengers needs
On time performance
Discipline in completing checks and inspections
Refuelling
As a pilot you are responsible to…
The Operator
Aircraft owner
Passengers
Owner of cargo
Public
Safety has been a prime consideration since almost the beginning of the air transport industry.
The regulators, manufacturers, operators and line pilots, who are the four main operating elements of the industry, have all done their best to minimize the risk of air accidents.
Unfortunately, there is no way to entirely eliminate this risk.
As technology advanced through the years the safety record of air transportation steadily improved.
During the mid seventies, the improvement reached a plateau and has remained essentially the same ever since.
Over 75% of aircraft accidents are attributable to or could have been prevented by human intervention.
This suggests that the greatest impact on flight safety must be achieved by improving human performance.
This led to the development and significance of the area called human factors in order to improve flight safety.
Human Factors is a general term that broadly encompasses aviation medicine, psychology and ergonomics.
Human Factors arose originally out of aircraft accident investigation.
Human Factors now extend beyond accident investigation.
Essentially moving towards human performance/limitation as a measure of accident prevention.
Is a license training requirement and designed to help understanding on human limitations.
Crew Resource Management
Threat and Error Management
Safety Management System
Compulsory Theory in Human Factors
Regulated Duty Times
Standard Operating Procedures
The effective use of all available resources for flight crew personnel.
CRM is concerned more towards the cognitive and interpersonal skills needed to manage the flight
Classroom training in CRM usually provided in conjunction with simulator revalidation training.
Threats and Errors are a part of everyday operations that carry out potential to generate undesired aircraft states.
At various stages in the chain of events, the flight crew may interrupt the process and avoid the development of an accident scenario.
Structured management approach to control safety risks in operations.
Specific processes related to safety of operations.
Applying a quality management approach to control safety risks.
Communicating and providing direction.
Physiology and the Effects of Flight
Daltons Law states that total pressure of a mixture of gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of each gas in the mixture.
As we gain altitude the percentage of oxygen remains the same.
Since total air pressure is decreasing so will oxygen partial pressure.
As altitude increases
Pressure and density decreases
Any decrease from 102mm Hg O2 in the lungs leads to impairment.
Circulation and Respiratory Systems
The process of respiration:
Brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide, this occurs in two stages.
1st stage external respiration occurring in the lungs.
2nd stage internal respiration taking place in the body tissues.
Permanent need for oxygen:
This is used in energy producing “burning” process that occurs in every cell of the body tissues.
Any prolonged interruption may lead to physical damage and possibly death.
Two separate lungs are housed within the chest cavity protected by the rib cage.
Below a muscular curved diaphragm can expand the chest cavity drawing fresh air.
Air is drawn through the bronchial passage which divides into 2 tubes, one going into each lung.
The 2 tubes divide into smaller and smaller tubes ending in a million small air sacs.
The Respiratory System – External Respiration
The region of the small sac is surrounded by blood capillaries.
Oxygen molecules diffuse through the alveoli into blood stream.
Attaches to haemoglobin in the red blood cells which have high affinity for oxygen to be transported around the body
Oxygen is brought to the body tissue by the red blood cells:
This then diffuses through the very thin capillary and body cell wall into the body.
Through a process called “oxidation”, food and liquid are chemically changed into energy.
Carbon Dioxide (CO2):
This is a waste product as a result of burning oxygen.
Carbon Dioxide then diffuses back into capillaries.
Then back to the lungs for external respiration.
The heart is a muscular pump, divided into two sides each with two chambers.
The muscles of the heart contract in a double action pulse, forcing blood through one-way valves through a network of arteries.
This pump causes a pressure pulse that can be felt at various part of the body.
Blood pressure is a measure of blood against the walls of the main arteries.
Systolic Peak Pressure.
Diastolic Lowest Pressure.
This moves blood around the body, carrying oxygen and nutrients to cells, and takes away waste products.
Blood: composed of plasma carrying red & white blood cells.
Red Blood Cells contain iron rich pigment haemoglobin, principal function is to transport oxygen.
White Blood Cells protect the body against foreign substances.
Platelets in the blood function to form clots when necessary to stop blood loss.
Blood vessels form a system of arteries, capillaries and veins.
Arteries carry blood into the body, away from the heart.
Veins carry blood back to the heart.
The smallest blood vessels are the capillaries, which enable an exchange of oxygen and other matter with individual cells in the body tissue.
The circulation of blood through the vessels and the tissues is known as systemic circulation.
A second system, the pulmonary circulation, diverts the blood that returns to the heart into capillaries situated in the walls of the air sacs.
The bloodstream passes through the lungs, which exchange the carbon dioxide from the blood and add oxygen to it.
Oxygenated blood returns to the heart.
Hypoxia
Hypoxia; a condition in which the amount of oxygen carried by the blood is reduced and becomes insufficient to meet tissue needs.
Caused by…
A decrease in oxygen partial pressure
Carbon Monoxide poisoning
Pilot Illness
Hypoxia can become so severe that a person becomes completely deprived of oxygen, this condition is anoxia.
The partial pressure of oxygen at sea level is 150mm Hg outside the lungs and 102mm Hg inside the lungs.
The gas exchange process in the lungs occurs due to the existing pressure differential between the capillary surface of the alveoli and the outside atmosphere.
If oxygen partial pressure is reduced, this differential is reduced, and less oxygen is forced into the blood.
Hypoxia Effects on the Brain
Behavioural: Loss of self criticism and judgment, euphoria, fatigue and lethargy, fixation, hyperventilating or sighing.
Visual: Reduced acuity, dimming, reduced peripheral vision then tunnel vision, reduced colour perception, reduced night vision.
Intellectual: reduced or lost memory, confusion, muddled thinking, unable to concentrate, detached and disorientated feeling.
Sensory: Headache, lightheadedness, dizziness, numbness and tingling of extremities, sweating and clamminess, hot and cold flushes.
Movement: Slight tremor becoming coarser and finally turning into an uncoordinated flapping of arms and hands. Clumsiness, muscular incoordination, unsteady gait.
Appearance: Paleness, increased drowsiness, bluing of the skin (particularly around lips and fingernails).
Hypoxia affects higher mental functions first, as brain tissues and eyes are most sensitive to oxygen deprivation.
So, detection of the onset of hypoxia can be difficult.
Euphoria + Poor Judgement = Danger
- Hypoxia will not affect all pilots in the same way.
Age
Physical fitness and / or illness
Lifestyle – Smoking, alcohol and other drug use
Training and recognition
Acclimatisation
Pressurised aircraft
Education about Hypoxia
Training and recognition
Use of supplemental oxygen
Defined as the time in which a person can be expected to take effective preventative measures.
15 to 30 minutes at 18,000ft
3 to 5 minutes at 25,000ft
45 to 60 seconds at 35,000ft
Time of safe consciousness is approximately 2 minutes.
Oxygen supplied immediately
Beware the “Oxygen Paradox”
Descent the aircraft
Someone who is mild to moderately Hypoxic, when placed on oxygen their symptoms may temporarily worsen
The cause is believed to be a momentary reflex constricting the effect on arteries to the brain, caused by the sudden increase in O2 in the blood stream.
The arteries will rapidly dilate again and rapidly return to normal
Hyperventilation is simply over-breathing which results in too much carbon dioxide being eliminated from the blood stream.
This result in symptoms such as:
Tingling
Visual Disturbances
Hot and cold flushes
Anxiety
Impaired performance
Loss of consciousness
Hyperventilation Video
Hypoxia can cause hyperventilation as the body tries to get more oxygen by increasing the rate of breathing.
Fear or panic can also trigger hyperventilation
An increased breathing rate due to exercise does not cause hyperventilation as the physical exertion generates extra CO2 in the body.
It can be difficult to tell the difference between hypoxia and hyperventilation; if in doubt supply oxygen.
Hyperventilation due to fear or high stress can be treated by breathing into a paper bag as this increases the CO2 levels in the blood.
If a person loses consciousness due to hyperventilation respiration will quickly return to normal. Loss of consciousness due to hypoxia will likely result in death.
Entrapped Gases
Trauma caused by trapped gases within the body expanding and contracting.
Because body temperature remains essentially constant and pressure drops with altitude, the volume of any gas entrapped within the body cavities increases.
Ear – gas can be trapped in the middle ear if the soft walls of the top of the Eustachian tube become swollen, such as with a cold.
Pressure inside the ear can then not equalize with outside pressure causing distortion of the ear drum.
This causes extreme pain and possible rupturing of the drum. This condition is known as ‘Otic Barotrauma’.
Sinuses – these are cavities within the skull above the eyes, in the cheeks and at the back of the nose.
If a person is suffering from a cold or allergy the soft tissues around these cavities can swell and mucus can also cause blockages to the openings preventing air from venting.
Teeth – gas pockets can occur in teeth due to poor fillings and dental abscesses, also resulting in severe pain.
Small Bowel – gas can form due to the fermentation of certain foods, if it is prevented from venting it can cause the bowel wall to stretch, resulting in severe pain.
In the training environment, problems are more likely to occur on the descent rather than climbing.
Even low powered aircraft can change altitude rapidly on descent, giving rise to rapid pressure changes.
Mildly blocked ears can normally be cleared by holding your nose and blowing hard, a manoeuvre known as the Valsalva Manoeuvre.
Chewing, swallowing or yawning can also help to equalize the pressure differential.
Don’t go flying if you are suffering from an illness e.g. a bad cold.
This occurs when a decrease in surrounding pressure causes the nitrogen in the blood to “bubble out” of solution.
These bubbles move freely around the body and become lodged in the joints, the brain, the spinal cord, and under the skin causing a variety of symptoms.
This could occur for pilots flying unpressurised aircraft above 18,000ft for prolonged periods. The higher you go the more likely you are to develop the bends.
Joint pain
Itchiness and numbness
Stomach pain
Tingling or sensation of movement in the skin
Paralysis/Loss of control of parts of the body
Breathing difficulties
Disturbances in vision: loss of acuity, flashes, blank areas
Co-ordination and movement problems
Unconsciousness
Permanent paralysis
Death
Prevention of “The Bends” in aviation requires the use of pressurized aircraft for higher altitude flights.
Time to wait before flying, after diving;
If possible don’t plan to fly for 24 Hours after last dive
12 hours if depth is 10 metres
24 hours if depth is 10-35 metres
48 hours if depth is greater than 35 metres
48 hours if diving and planning to fly 8-10,000ft
It should also be noted that elderly and overweight pilots will be more susceptible to the bends.
Treatment is urgent compression in a dive chamber.
Once the bends have developed a person must not ascend to a height of more than 500ft AMSL cabin pressure before receiving treatment
Although an unlikely scenario it would cause tremendous noise, instant fog, extreme cold and flying debris.
The effect on the body would be severe pain in the ears, sinuses, and stomach. Also, air from your stomach would be expelled and useful consciousness would be a matter of seconds.
It would be vital to go onto 100% oxygen ASAP and begin an emergency descent.
Explosive Decompression Video
Cornea – Transparent cap over the lens through which light rays pass. Some refraction occurs and provides the coarse focus.
Iris – Between the cornea and lens a colored membrane known as the Iris.
Pupil – At the centre of the iris a small round aperture known as the pupil. Changes its size to restrict the amount of light entering the lens.
Lens – Transparent, changes shape with ciliary muscles allowing to focus the light rays. Greater curvature means greater focusing i.e, objects near you.
Retina – Light sensitive layer located at the back of eye. Essentially the screen onto which the lens focuses image on. 2 types of light sensitive cells in the retina.
Cones – Found in central foveal region. Sensitive to colour, details and distant objects.
Rods – Concentrated in a band outside the foveal area. Sensitive to movement but not detail or colour and therefore can only see black and white.
Optic Nerve – These images are converted into electrical signals that pass along the optic nerve.
Complex process involving looking, seeing and recognition, using the eye and parts of the brain.
Cones receive bright light energy, and are situated mainly in the centre of the retina, allowing sharp vision of finer details and the registration of colour.
Rods react to low level light, they are more widely distributed with fewer in the centre, and detect movement better than the cones, particularly in peripheral vision.
Having two eyes allows 3D vision out to about 10m.
Empty Field Myopia – can occur in condition of low visual stimulus; the eye take up its relaxed focal length of 3 to 4 metres.
Discerning objects in daylight – Crossing wires. Use of cones for fine detail.
Luminance – Arising from the object itself or due to reflection, determines how well an object can be seen. Too much causes “Glare”.
Contrast – Difference between the object and background, nil contrast means an object cannot be seen.
Colour Perception – Requires high luminance so cones are in use.
The Blind Spot – one in each eye where the optic nerve leave the retina.
Aircraft Cut Off on Final
Most night flying is carried out under IFR.
It is possible to fly visually at night by using light references on the ground.
Dark Adaption – the eye can adapt to low levels of light and will be 50% adapted after 10 mins and fully adapted after 30 mins.
Once adapted, night vision will be rapidly destroyed by sudden exposure particularly white light.
Precautionary Actions to protect night vision:
Instrument lights on dim
Avoid looking directly at light source of high illuminance i.e. look at from side on
Torch required to be carried by law, use red lighting as it doesn’t deteriorate night vision as much as white light.
Strobes and landing lights off if not required, such as on the ground.
Long-sightedness (Hyperopia)
Trouble focusing on close objects
Short-sightedness (Myopia)
Trouble focusing on objects far away
Presbyopia
Long sightedness due to aging
Astigmatism
The front surface of the eye or the lens inside the eye is curved differently in one direction than the other
A common symptom is blurry vision
Pilots can wear corrective lenses while flying, but there are certain requirements that must be met.
Civil Aviation Rules – Medical Examiner Manual Part 3.
Spare spectacles readily available.
Use of contact lenses, good tolerance after a period of adaption must be demonstrated.
Recommended the use of neutral grey/green/brown tint to avoid altered perception of surroundings.
The use of transition lenses is discouraged.
Must not be used by night.
If using corrective sunglasses by day, clear space spectacles to be carried.
The use of polarized lenses is not recommended.
Polarised lenses diminish glare by absorbing and blocking incoming horizontal light, while allowing in vertical light.
This reduces the ability to read instruments that already incorporate anti-glare filters.
This also interferes with the ability to read LCD instruments, which emit polarized light.
Polarised lenses interfere with seeing out the aircraft’s windscreen by enhancing striations in laminated materials.
Empty Field Myopia
Flying in conditions of low visual stimulus a form of “short sightedness” can occur.
Low visual stimulus field is where pilot’s visual field is relatively unbroken by distinctive features e.g. low vis, broken cloud, sky clear.
Short sightedness occurs because unless the eye is stimulated by objects within its field of view.
It will tend to take up its natural relaxed focal length of approximately 3-4 metres.
The process of vision is not instantaneous, and in fact takes approximately 1.5 seconds.
20 degrees, 2 second rule – a scanning technique to allow the eye to focus.
EFM can be overcome by consciously and frequently shifting focus and stretching the focal length.
With 2 pilots divide the search area but allow an overlap.
Fundamental for VFR flight is keeping a good lookout. Sighting cloud/traffic and terrain is key to avoiding these obstacles.
However, the time taken from looking, to providing a course of action to avoid includes some intermediate steps.
Looking 1 – 0.2 secs
Seeing 2 – 0.3 secs
Recognising 0.7 – 1.0 secs
Evaluating/Deciding 2.0 – 3.0 secs
Action 2.0 – 3.0 secs
Total Time 5.0 – 7.5 secs
If at night, a pilot looks directly at a dim single point light source, the light may disappear and reappear giving an apparent movement.
At night, the rods are critical for vision and there are fewer of them in the centre of the retina.
Furthermore, it will often begin to have apparent movement intermittently as it is sensed by the rods in the peripheral vision.
Also called the stroboscopic illumination illusion.
This occurs when a bright light source is intermittently and rapidly interrupted, such as looking at the setting sun through a propeller.
It can cause dizziness; making you as the pilot feel unwell or even causing a seizure. If this does occur look away, use a sunshade or reposition the aircraft.
Flicker Vertigo; Jetranger Helicopter Video
When flying in condition of low visual stimulus, including at night and often with a low workload, a phenomenon known as “break off” can occur.
This occurs at high altitude, hazy conditions, solo pilot conditions, when the aircraft is on autopilot etc.
The break off phenomenon has been described as being psychologically detached from one’s surroundings.
It may be experienced as a feeling of “being outside the cockpit looking in”.
“Break Off” is not long lasting or has any major consequences but may be more common in pilots who are naturally more anxious by nature.
Flying an approach to a runway with no visible ground features can be difficult.
This can occur when approach a runway on a dark night where the only lights visible are the runway edge lights.
The problem that arises is that with no visual ground features, visual judgement of height above the ground will be difficult on the approach, particularly the undershoot area.
The tendency; to think that the aircraft is higher than what you actually are.
This results in an urge to push the nose down and fly a shallower approach.
Perception: The way in which something is regarded, understood, or interpreted.
Visual errors can occur when different factors alter perception.
False Horizon can occur at times such as:
Sloping surface lights at night mistake to be level.
Sloping cloud layers mistaken to be level.
Sloping terrain mistaken to be level.
Pilots rely heavily on being able to see the Earth’s horizon for orientation.
If the horizon becomes distorted or diminished, the pilot will lose a major visual reference for orientation.
This may lead the pilot to create a false horizon and interpret an incorrect sense of orientation.
Furthermore, the pilot may rely on other senses such as, balance, hearing, pressures etc. Which is an unreliable source of orientation.
The motion of an object with respect to other moving/stationary objects is called “relative motion”.
One of the most powerful cues to detecting an object is if it moves relative to its surrounding – hence why animals freeze when they feel threatened.
If two aircraft have a constant relative bearing, there will be a lack of relative motion between the aircraft and its surrounding image.
Fog: is the term used when the visibility is less than 1000m and is effectively cloud in contact with the surface.
Haze: is any obstruction in visibility due to dust, smoke or particles in the air.
These phenomenon dimmish the horizon and affects visual reference for orientation.
Furthermore, they reduce visual range making flying under VFR conditions difficult to unattainable.
Reduced visibility will be much worse if the pilot has a dirty or badly scratched windscreen effectively simulating poor visibility and obstructing the field of view.
Essential in terms of flight safety to look after aircraft windscreens.
Clean vertically rather than horizontally as a horizontal scratch makes it more difficult to detect aircraft.
Important to use cleaning agent that will not scratch Perspex or glass.
A steep approach makes the runway appear longer and narrower.
A low approach makes the runway appear shorter and wider.
Learning to recognize the correct shape and perspective is an important part of learning to fly.
Longer Runway – the correct perspective will appear like a steep approach. The tendency of the pilot will then be to get too low on approach.
Shorter Runway – the correct perspective will appear like a shallow approach. The tendency of the pilot will then be to get too high on approach.
Wider – appearance of being low, tendency to get high.
Narrow – appearance of being high, tendency to get low.
Down Slope – the pilot will think he/she is low and make a higher-than-normal approach.
Up Slope – the pilot will think he/she is high and make a lower-than-normal approach.
Runway light intensity – brighter lights make you think you are closer than you actually are.
Different textures can make judgement of the round-out and flare on landing more difficult.
Differences between landing surfaces like bitumen, grass, gravel and water can affect judgement of height above ground
The correct perspective can alter with different runway lengths, slope, width and texture
Glassy Water Landing Illusion Video
Hearing and Balance
The ear provides 2 vital senses – Hearing and Balance
Hearing allow us to interpret sound
Signals caused by pressure vibrations through the air as pressure waves.
These cause sensitive membranes like the ear drums to vibrate.
The balance organs tell us:
Which way is up
Whether we are moving at a constant speed or accelerating.

lessons.title: Anatomy of the Ear – Outer Ear

content.content: Pinna or Auricle – the external section used to gather sound signals.
Outer Canal – is the section through which pressure waves pass.
Eardrum – caused to vibrate in harmony with the pressure waves.

lessons.title: Anatomy of the Ear – Middle Ear

content.content: Air filled cavity maintained at ambient pressure via the Eustachian Tube.
Contains 3 small bones arranged to amplify the vibration of the eardrum called the Ossicles.
This vibration is passed onto the cochlea, a section in the inner ear.
There is no leakage of air across the eardrum.
Any interference to movement of ossicles will reduce/distort the sound signals commonly associated by infections or a blocked eustachian tube.

lessons.title: Anatomy of the Ear – Inner Ear

content.content: Cochlea: Vibrations from the Ossicles causes movement of fluid in the cochlea. This then causes hair-like cells that protrude into the fluid to convert vibrations into electrical signals.

Vestibular Apparatus: This consists of 3 fluid filled ‘Semicircular Canals’ each with a cluster of small hairs at their base. Interactions between the fluid in the canals and the hairs provide sensations of movement in the three axis of flight.
Otolithic Organ (Utricle): A device that detects linear accelerations and whether we are up right or not.
Prolonged exposure to noise can cause damage to the Cochlea in the inner ear. The amount of damage will depend on the level of noise and length of exposure.
Sound intensity is measured in ‘Decibels’ which is a logarithmic scale; for every 20dB the sound level increases ten-fold and the sound energy by hundred-fold.
A noise induced hearing loss may develop gradually over a period of years without the person noticing and this is commonly irreversible.
Ear plugs can reduce noise by about 20dB.
Earmuffs can reduce noise by about 40dB.
Active noise cancelling headsets generate a ‘counter wave’ that blanks out almost all noise entirely.
Exposure to high levels of noise, around 130dB, will cause pain.
Exposure to 140dB or more will cause instantaneous damage.
Exposure to moderate noise, 90 to 100 dB for prolonged periods will cause a temporary reduction in hearing ability. Hearing will return to normal within a few days if noise is avoided.
Exposure to 80 to 85 dB over a normal 40hr working week should have no effect.
As mentioned, this can occur due to noise exposure without protection.
Presbycusis – Hearing loss due to aging, particularly of higher frequencies.
Hearing Loss can be attributed to a number of reasons:
Damage to the auditory nerve
Mechanical damage to the bones in the middle ear or to the eardrum
Ear infections or other illness
Hereditary or birth defects
Some antibiotics and anit-malarial drugs can cause tinnitus and/or permanent deafness.
When the pressure outside the ear changes, the eardrum will flex towards the low pressure, whether that be outside the ear or in the inner ear.
The pressure will equalize between the inner ear and outside pressure through the Eustachian Tube.
If this equalization cannot take place, the eardrum may distort to the point that it ruptures.
Colds and Sinusitis can block the Eustachian tube and sinus cavities.
This prevents the pilot from being able to equalize the pressure inside and out during a climb or descent.
Intense pain and possible ruptured eardrum could occur.
Never fly when you have a cold or sinus infection.
Be aware that hayfever and allergies can have the same effect on the inner ear and sinus cavities as a cold.
Spatial Orientation
Spatial Orientation
Is the ability to determine your attitude in relation to the Earth.
Usually achieved by a combination of three senses:
Vision
Vestibular system
Proprioceptive system
Which one of these senses is the most reliable?
Disorientation
The condition of having lost one’s sense of direction.
Spatial Disorientation
Not knowing your attitude in relation to the horizon (e.g. which way is up).
There are certain parts within the inner ear which the body uses for orientation, sometimes referred to as the balance organs.
Consists of 3 fluid filled canals which are arranged at right angles to each other.
They sense angular acceleration, i.e. change of direction, in the 3 different planes.
Once the acceleration has stopped or become constant the canals will no longer sense anything.
Also called the Otolith Organs.
These are located next to the semi-circular canals and act as accelerometers to sense head tilt and longitudinal acceleration.
Verticality is detected by sensory hairs in a sac filled with gelatinous material.
The sacs outer membrane is studded with small crystals of calcium carbonate called otoliths and give the organ its name.
Movement of the hair cells sends a message to the brain.
However, the movement can misinterpret forward acceleration as a head tilt backwards.
This is the pressure/stretch/position nervous system often referred to as the “seat of the pants”.
It consists of pressure are receptors, muscle-stretch receptors and limb position receptors which send signals to the brain.
The pressure receptors are the most important as the body’s “g-meter”.

lessons.title: Interconnection of Vision and Vestibular Systems

content.content: Occulogyral Reflex
There is a strong reflex interconnection between the eyes and the balance organs.
This allows accurate visual tracking of objects even when the body and head are moving rapidly or unevenly.
Ear infections in the ear can lead to an uncomfortable dizziness and loss of balance called Vertigo
If we remove the visual system, our reliance becomes on the vestibular and proprioceptive systems to maintain our orientation.
These two systems are not reliable without vision aiding them and disorientation can occur.
The semi-circular canals require a certain level of stimulation to work.
Any acceleration below this threshold (sub-threshold stimulation) will not register.
For example, entering a level turn with a small angle of bank while instrument flying.
Without visual reference this can lead to the pilot thinking he/she is level when actually in a turn.
An example of an accident caused by this illusion is an aircraft accelerating from 100 to 130 knots in 10 seconds, this generates an acceleration on the pilot of 0.16G.
This acceleration is sufficient enough to produce the sensation of a 9-degree pitch up.
More commonly associated with take-offs on a dark night where visual cues are less obvious.
Pilots with limited recent night or instrument flying experience appear more susceptible to this spatial disorientation.
Often because they may not be fully accustomed to these misleading acceleration sensations.
This is a false sensation of rotation.
The sense of turning (aircraft being banked) stops after about 10 secs after a turn is established.
When wings are returned to level there is a strong sense of turning in the opposite direction when the turn is stopped.
A classic example of this is the ‘Graveyard Spiral’, where the illusion of an opposite direction turn after returning to S&L.
Both sensations are illusions and are readily over-ridden by visual horizon cues.
Acceleration into the spin causes the fluid in the semi-circular canals to register a rotation.
As the spin continues, this sensation begins to disappear.
When the spin is stopped (wings level), the semi-circular canals will register acceleration in the opposite direction.
The pilot may then try to recover from this perceived spin in the opposite direction (even though they are actually straight and level).
This can lead to complete disorientation, the only way to recover is for the pilot to refer to the instruments to realise the wings need to be levelled before pulling out of the dive.
Generally occurs when a pilot is in bank and bends the head downward or backward (e.g. to pick up a dropped checklist).
The turn activates one semicircular canal, and the head movement activates another canal.
The simultaneous stimulation of two or more semicircular canals produces an almost unbearable sensation that the aircraft is rolling, pitching and yawing all at the same time.
This sensation is similar to rolling down a hillside.
The specific sensation is called Vertigo, and it can quickly disorient a pilot and cause a significant loss in aircraft control and judgement.
A form of vertigo triggered by the collapse of the eardrums, this is typically due to a blocked Eustachian Tube.
This can occur when flying with a head cold or with blocked sinuses.
As pressure changes occur, such as climbing or descending, the eardrum may become perforated and nausea and/or vertigo are the result.
Pilot who are unaware of the causes and factors involved with spatial illusions will be more susceptible to disorientation.
For prevention of illusions such as the leans, somatgravic and somatogyral illusions, the key is “Trust your instruments!”.
For illusions such as Coriolis effect – keep you head movements to a minimum and again refer to your instruments as a primary means of indicating orientation.
For Pressure Vertigo – never go flying while you are sick, control the rate of descent if possible to prevent quick changes in pressure.
Gravitational Forces
Blood is forced downwards depriving the brain and eyes of oxygen.
Loss of colour vision – Grey out
Loss of peripheral vision – Tunnel vision
Loss of visual acuity – Blurring vision
Total loss of vision – Black out
Eventually leading to a loss of consciousness due to excessvice G loading:
G-LOC
Blood is forced into the head and has difficulty returning to the heart.
This prevents newly oxygenated blood from getting into the brain and eyes.
This lack of oxygen will reduce brain and visual functionality.
Red Out – blood collecting in and around the eyes and eyelids.
When you red out, the impression is of a total loss of vision due to the red veil of blood blocking normal eyesight.
Tolerance to negative G’s is much less than for positive.
Normal body, heart and blood vessel reflexes can cope up approximately 2.5 ‘G’s.
This compensation takes several seconds to occur and is known as the physiological compensation.
If the G-Force comes on at a fast rate or increases further, then technique must be used to increase the ‘G’ tolerance to avoid the previously mentioned symptoms from occurring.
Anti-G Straining Manoeuvre
Tightening or isometrically straining leg, chest and abdominal muscles.
Increasing arterial blood pressure by pressurizing the chest
This is achieved by isometrically straining the muscles in the chest, neck and shoulders.
G Suit application, recency and continued practice.
Being short or stocky
Weight (anaerobic) training.
Lack of recency
Poor Anti-G straining technique
Poorly fitting G-Suit
Illness, dehydration, hangover, drugs or hypoxia
Aerobic training
Being too tall
Having low blood pressure
Hyperventilation
Fatigue and heat stress
Motion Sickness
Caused by prolonged motion of the body which upsets the orientation systems by overloading them.
In conjunction with contradictory information between the visual and vestibular system.
Particularly affects the Occulogyral Reflex.
Effects include nausea, paleness, clammy skin, cold sweats and vomiting.
Exposure and desensitization.
Medication – not recommended for long term use.
Herbal remedies and pressure wrist bands.
Keeping the horizon in sight.
Gaining experience and thus reducing anxiety while building confidence.
Staying relaxed.
Avoid flying in rough weather, particularly turbulence or stormy conditions.
Keeping fit, exercising regularly.
Avoid getting over-tired.
Eating sensibly and avoiding alcohol.
When beginning any sort of aerobatic flight, keeping them short to start with.
Remove yourself from the situation in the first place, i.e. land the aircraft as soon as possible.
Breathe fresh cold air, open vents in the aircraft and let fresh air blow onto the face and neck.
Cool yourself down – putting cold water on your wrists or a cold towel on the forehead will help achieve this.
Look outside at the horizon ahead of you and try to keep your head as still as possible.
Enquire into a desensitization programme.
Flight Anxiety
Stress:
This is defined as a reaction to adverse environmental conditions called stressors.
Caused by external or internal factors that initially prepare the human for fight or flight.
Left unresolved, it can cause serious long term problems.
Anxiety:
The extreme worry that results when a person is emotionally overloaded, particularly for prolonged periods.
It is the state of being uneasy, apprehensive or worried about what ‘might’ happen.
Generalised experience is associated with pervasive and often unreasonable fear.
Flight anxiety can occur in ab-initio pilot as well as very experienced pilots too.
As well as a feeling of fear, physiological symptoms can occur also; headache, palpitations, breathing difficulties, dizziness and panic attacks.
Experienced pilots can suffer from anxiety on returning to flying duties after an accident for example.
This may also be classed as being a part of ‘Post Traumatic Stress Disorder’ or PTSD.
An anxious person will likely perform poorly and often becomes apparent through signs of:
Physical discomfort
Perspiring, nervous twitching, dry mouth breathing difficulties.
Panting, increased heart rate, shaking hands.
Inappropriate behaviour
Laughing, smiling or singing even at inappropriate times.
Extreme over-cooperation, rapid changes in emotion and impulsivity.
Knowledge
The more you know about a subject, the less you will fear it.
Counselling
Those who have been involved in an accident may need some type of counselling or therapy to help deal with their anxiety.
Lifestyle
Ensure you are getting adequate rest, exercise or time away to relax.

lessons.title: Fitness to Fly and Legal Requirements

content.content: A pilot must be: mentally and physically well in order to cope with the demands of the flying environment
A pilot must be free of any: illness, disability or other factor which could interfere with their ability to operate the aircraft safely.
This also entails: an awareness of health and lifestyle and being aware of when he/she is not fit to fly.
There is a legal requirement in achieving fitness to operate an aircraft by passing and keeping a current Aviation Medical through an approved Aviation Medical Examiner.
The purpose of a medical exam is to exclude medical conditions that are incompatible with safe flying practices.
It is your responsibility to visit your AME doctor if changes to your health may invalidate your ability to hold a medical certificate. This includes symptoms that involve:
Brain Function
Consciousness
Pain in chest
Respiratory Problems
Significant changes in vision
An AME can also tell you which medications are acceptable for Pilots to be taking while flying.

In 2004, an accident occurred where a Cessna AgWagon crashed shortly after takeoff. It was discovered that the pilot had suffered an incapacitating cardiac event which caused him to lose control of the aircraft.

His Class 1 Aviation Medical certificate had expired, he stated he was a non-smoker (even though he did smoke). This meant the appropriate tests weren’t conducted that would’ve picked up these cardiac issues.
Always be honest with your AME!
There is no known physiological reason that prevents female pilots from flying while pregnant as long as:
They remain healthy and there is no deterioration to normal everyday health and activity and;
Regular medical checks are being completed
Common problems associated with pregnant pilots are:
Anemia
Nausea
Tiredness
Low blood pressure
When not to fly:
After the 6th month it is recommended to discontinue flying
Passengers require permission from their Doctor to travel by air within the last 4 weeks of pregnancy.
Aerobatics and other vigorous maneuvers should be avoided.
Coronary Artery Disease
This develops when the major blood vessels become damaged or diseased.
Cholesterol-containing deposits (plaque) in your arteries and inflammation are usually to blame for coronary artery disease.
This narrows your coronary arteries and therefore decreases blood flow to your heart.
Symptoms include:
Chest pain (Angina)
Shortness of breath
Heart Attack
Cerebrovascular Disease
This relates to the brain and its blood vessels.
If a blockage or haemorrhage prevents the brain cells from getting enough oxygen, brain damage can result.
Detecting the symptoms:
Face drooping
Arm weakness
Speech difficulty
Time to call 111
Coronary Artery Disease is the forerunner to a heart attack
Heart attacks occur when one or more of the coronary arteries suddenly become blocked or unable to supply sufficient blood to the heart muscle. Severe chest pain is generally associated.
Unless rectified quickly, the lack of oxygen to the heart will cause part of the muscle to die, this is called Infarction.
Depending on the extent of the infarction, the heart’s function can become seriously impaired and even stop altogether.
1/3 of all deaths in NZ are caused by a cardiovascular disease.
Family history of heart disease
Smoking
Elevated blood pressure – Hypertension
Elevated blood cholesterol level
Lack of exercise and obesity
High blood sugar – Diabetes Mellitus
High levels of stress
These factors are cumulative, so the more you have, the more likely you are to suffer a heart attack.

Risk of cardiovascular disease can be reduced by: not smoking, eating a balanced diet, exercising regularly, reducing stress levels and avoiding diabetes and high cholesterol by dieting and exercising properly.
This is the reading of peak (Systolic) and resting (Diastolic) pressures of blood from the output side of the heart.
Normal blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg.
The acceptable range for peak pressure is 150 – 100 mm Hg, and for resting pressure is 95 – 60 mm Hg.
Blood pressure can change in response to body activity and position, temperature, emotional change, dehydration, stimulants, alcohol and illness.
High blood pressure is one of the prime causes of hardening of the arteries.
Lifestyle changes are required to reduce high blood pressure; increased fitness, healthy diet, reducing coffee, salt and alcohol intake, reducing stress, and reducing weight.
Reducing your weight is one of the most effective methods of reducing blood pressure.
High blood pressure can also be managed with medication.
Eating and drinking sensibly is advisable if you wish to fly right through to retirement age.
Going on a ‘crash diet’ is not recommended for pilots.
Long term lifestyle changes are the better option.
Diet pills and other weight loss medications are also not advisable.
Activity that increases the heart/lung fitness
Minimum of 3 times a week
Raises your heart rate to 1.5 times it’s resting rate, for at least 30 mins
Think carefully before playing contact sport which could result in a loss of your medical due to injury.
A condition where the energy reserves stored in the fatty tissues exceeds healthy limits.
Obesity is linked to numerous life-threatening illnesses.
It is avoided through healthy lifestyle choices.
Generally regarded as a BMI of 30kg/m2 or more.
The two major health effects of smoking are, increased risk of lung cancer and cardiovascular disease.
Regular smokers live between 2.5 to 10 years less on average than non-smokers, with men being affected more.
Numerous other cancers are also typically associated with smoking.
Further health effects include emphysema, impotence, cataracts, stroke and many other diseases.
Sinusitis
Inflammation or swelling of the tissue lining the sinuses. When blocked and filled with fluid, germs can grow and cause an infection.
Hay Fever
Causes congestion of the nose and sinuses similarly to the common cold.
Influenza
The influenza virus infects your nose, throat and lungs. The Flu is normally worse than a cold.
Asthma
A chronic condition in which the airway occasionally constricts, becomes inflamed and lined with excessive mucus.
This can range from mild to life threatening and generally controlled by medication.
An intestinal infection marked by severe diarrhoea, cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever.
Caused most often by infection with certain viruses, and less often by bacteria, parasites or reaction to diet/medication.
Sources of infection are often improperly prepared or reheated food, or contaminated water.
Crew incapacitation due to gastroenteritis will make them very weak an is sometimes common when travelling abroad.
Drink only bottled water (not necessary in most parts of New Zealand).
Beware of uncooked foods which may have been washed in tap water.
Seafood, dairy and bakery products are also high risk so take caution with these.
Be careful about where you are eating.
Treatment for Gastroenteritis is immediate rehydration and replacement of lost electrolytes. Avoid flying for at least 72 hours after the last symptoms, even in the case of mild food poisoning.
People who suffer from seizures or epilepsy will not obtain a medical certificate.
Brain injuries may result in temporary or permanent loss of your medical certificate.
Fainting – the cause would need to be established as it may be the symptom of another problem.
Headaches/Migraines – if these are debilitating you will not be able to hold a medical certificate.
Any factor which could possibly result in sudden incapacitation of a pilot will disqualify that person from obtaining or keeping their medical certificate.
Clinical depression is a serious psychiatric disorder. It may be isolated or as a secondary result of some other illness.
The cause can be physiological or psychological and there are many different types of depression.
Symptoms can include persistent sadness, loss of appetite, insomnia, feeling of worthlessness, difficulty remembering or making decisions, suicidal thoughts.
As can be seen from the symptoms, a person suffering from depression should not be acting as Pilot in Command of an aircraft.
If you suspect you are suffering from depression or anxiety, seek help; it is very treatable and often provides resounding success when helped.
Alcohol in the blood impairs one’s performance with the added danger of suppressing anxiety and removing inhibitions.
Consumption severely affects judgement, ability, whilst misleading the pilot to think they are performing well.
Furthermore, it represses social morals and allows emotions and lowered standards of behavior to occur.
Duration: Alcohol can have lasting effects in the brain even once the blood alcohol level has returned to zero.
12 Hours ‘bottle to throttle’ is the minimum recommended time that must be observed after LIGHT alcohol consumption.
Determining factor for flying is that the pilot should be free of any alcohol symptoms and fit to fly.
Each person will react to alcohol differently, factors like type of consumption, duration of consumption, food intake and body weight will affect everyone slightly different.
Alcoholic: someone who’s excessively drinking, repeatedly damages their physical, mental, social and professional life.
The Hangover:
Heavy drinking can result in effects lasting much longer than the bottle to throttle rule
The Hangover effect can last 48 hours or more
Time before flying
Light drinking – 12 hours bottle to throttle
Heavy drinking pilots should wait at least double the time it takes for the blood alcohol level to reach zero, before flying.
Assessment for IMSAFE must be until the pilot is no longer affected by the alcohol, however self judgement can sometimes be difficult.
Alcoholism
A pilot diagnosed as an alcoholic must be immediately grounded. Alcoholism results in an instant loss of your medical. Reinstatement only occurs if the pilot completes a Rehabilitation programme.
All drugs affect the body as well as the virus, disease, infection they are combatting. However, side effects can occur.
Half lives: drugs that when their concentration stays too high for long periods of time e.g. sleeping pills.
Potentiating agents: Drugs that change or exaggerate the effects of other drugs when taken together, particularly alcohol.
Some medication can be incompatible with flying, such as:
Antihistamines: used to combat colds and hay fever can cause issues with drowsiness and alertness.
Antibiotics: E.g. Penicillin used to combat infection, however the disease itself might cause issues.
Tranquilisers: anti-depressants and sedatives.
Stimulants: used to maintain wakefulness or suppress appetite.
Anaesthetics: local anaesthetic usually requires 24 hours before flying, while general anaesthetic at least 72 hours.
Generally, drugs should be avoided while flying.
Any drugs being used for the first time should be trialed on the ground first. Unless cleared by a Doctor, it is safe to assume any drug or medication will temporarily or permanently ground you.
In general, drugs that are considered safe include ones that are:
Mild and have predictable responses
Have no known serious side effects which affect the brain or nervous system, including paracetamol, aspirin, antacids, nasal sprays and decongestants
The reason for medication should also be considered in your decision as to whether you are safe to fly.
Heroin, cocaine and Opium radically effect the CNS (Central Nervous System) as well as, mood and mental functioning and can permanently damage the brain.
Historically heavy drug use can lead to addiction and possibly death.
Cannabis: linked to heavier addicitons and degraded performance in motor and coordination skills.
A pilot should never take ‘recreational’ drugs. Mixing of drugs and alcohol is incredibly dangerous also.
Blood donation is an important service, but pilots must take care when doing so.
Donating blood can reduce the circulating volume which can then lead to low blood pressure and fainting.
It can also reduce tolerance to Hypoxia and G-Forces.
After 1 Unit of donation (600mL) a period of 24 hours must elapse before flying.
Environmental Hazards
The gas is colourless, odourless and is high poisonous.
Where does Carbon Monoxide come from?
This can enter the cockpit through a leaking exhaust or faulty heater.
Haemoglobin
Helps facilitate oxygen flow in your blood stream to your organs.
Carbon Monoxide binds strongly to your Haemoglobin however.
Blood will go from red to a cherry-purple colour
Detection:
Part of aircraft maintenance is to check for CO leaks.
Detection kits can be installed consisting of a colour-sensitive reagent marker.
It is a legal requirement to have a CO detector fitted to an aircraft.
Symptoms include:
Corrective actions:
Supplemental oxygen if available
Eliminate the source if possible, turn off cabin heater
Increase cabin ventilation
Land as soon as possible
Full rich mixture CO content
This will produce about 8% carbon monoxide by weight in the exhaust gasses and cruise power settings give around 3%.
Inhalation:
If 0.06% is inhaled, you will be unconscious after 2 hours.
A concentration of 0.1% can result in death after only 1 hour.

Example accident: In 2002, a PPL licensed Pilot went for a flight in his homebuilt aircraft. The aircraft was seen to be flying low level when it banked steeply then entered a spin before crashing into the ground. The pilot made no attempt to recover, and the autopsy revealed a 23% concentration of carbon monoxide in the blood. It was revealed that the pilot had repositioned the heating duct over a slip joint in the exhaust.
Avgas contains lead which can be absorbed into the blood stream when splashed on the skin or into the mouth and eyes. Prolonged exposure can cause lead poisoning.
Avgas can have narcotic and anesthetic effects on the nervous system, including the nose so the pilot loses their sense of smell.
Kerosene, Jet A1, Diesel, Avgas and Hydraulic Oils can also be very harmful to the skin itself.
Fuel can cause irritation to the eyes, throat and stomach. Leading to headache, nausea, excitement, blurred vision, confusion and lack of coordination.
De-icing Fluids
Fire extinguishers other than dry powder types
Insecticides and herbicides used in agricultural spraying
Paint and glues used in building or fixing aircraft
Avoid exposure with protective clothing, use of appropriate containers and adherence to instructors on use and handling.
Stress Management
Stress
This is defined as a reaction to adverse environmental conditions called stressors.
Arousal
This is defined as the general level of activity or performance.
This is measured on a scale from extreme drowsiness to frantic overactivity.
Optimum Performance
This occurs at a level between the two extremes.
Stressors can increase arousal beyond that level resulting in decreased performance.
Duration
This can be acute (short term) or chronic (long term).
Flying Environment
A direct stressor like weather, nose or aircraft performance
Operational
These overlap with the environmental stressors
Include flight planning, single pilot operations, crew cooperation, navigation, flight length etc.
Life / Domestic
Relationship problems, financial hardship, job security etc.
Work
Workload, shiftwork, relationships with colleagues, career advancement, work culture/climate etc.
Temperature
Above 30⁰C or below 13⁰C will impair performance
Heat will cause increased heart rate and blood pressure, sweating, attention problems.
Cold temperatures can cause discomfort and loss of feeling in the extremities.
To minimize, try to control environmental temperatures and stay hydrated.
Humidity
Excessive humidity increases the effects of heat. High humidity does not lead hydration but can be discomforting and can also lead to increased stress.
Low humidity can cause drying of the eyes, nose and throat, plus dehydration. Humidity in the cockpit can fall as low as 5% with 40-60% being comfort range.
Social stresses in the tropics are noticeable in the wet season with crime, alcoholism, divorce rate increasing dramatically.
Noise
Noise is unwanted sound energy with industry limit for continuous noise being 85dB.

If loud enough or present for prolonged periods, it can cause damage to hearing. Furthermore, unwanted noise can be distracting, irritable and stress inducing. With excessive noise, Pilot’s attention become narrow and shallow.
A busy day on the radio may adversely impact a person’s attention by interference through their thought process.
Vibrations
Transmitted to the body from the aircraft via the airframe, seat or seat belts.
Can cause discomfort, distraction and fatigue.
Severe vibrations can make it difficult to read instruments, maps or look outside.
To manage vibrations, additional cushioning, wearing heavier clothing and avoiding contact with the airframe is advisable.
AirAsiaX A330 Vibration Video

lessons.title: Acute and Chronic Physiological Effects of Stress

content.content: Acute:
Pupil dilation
Dry mouth
Sweating
Flight or fight response – increased blood pressure, increased respiration, blood vessels in skin contract, adrenaline release, liver releases glucose.
Tensed muscles
Digestion slows
Chronic:
Blurred vision, Asthma, Fatigue, Ulcers, indigestion, constipation
Trouble swallowing
Headaches, dizziness, migraines, insomnia, nightmares
Excessive blood sugar
High blood pressure and cardiovascular problems
Feeling of dissatisfaction
Aggression
Depression
Moodiness and irritability
Forgetfulness
Indecision
Narrowing of attention
Reduced working memory
Regression to earlier learned behaviours or responses
Typical signs of stress that can be observed include:
Short temperedness
Making mistakes
Taking up smoking or even drugs
Excessive drinking of alcohol
Uncharacteristic behaviour or a change in someone’s demeanor
Physical:
Being fit and healthy
Eating sensibly and regularly
Sleeping well and going flying with plenty of rest
Controlling your environment; temperature, noise and vibration
Psychological:
Being well prepared regarding knowledge
Being proud of your professional and personal qualities
Leaving your domestic and financial worries at home
Avoid procrastinating and discuss your worries or doubts
Don’t undertake unnecessary risks
Breathing Exercises:
Take deep slow breaths while focusing on relaxing your muscles
Whole body relaxation:
Lie down comfortably and starting at your feet first tense your muscles then relax them. Progress all the way up your body.
Meditation:
Comes in many forms and works best if done regularly for 15 ro 20 minutes at a time.
Sleep is a behavioural state that is a natural part of every individual’s life.
We spend about one-third of our lives asleep.
People generally know little about the importance of this essential activity.
Sleep is a required activity and is important for normal motor and cognitive function.
Most adults require a minimum of 8 hours of sleep every 24 hours.
Babies and small children require much more, and elderly people often find they need less sleep.
The requirement is not the same for everyone and it is important you have an idea of your own requirement.
How will these factors affect coping with environmental stressors?
Biological Clock
“Sleep wakefulness rhythms”
Internal mechanism which controls body functions
Natural time span of 25-26 hours
Zeitgebers
Rhythmically occurring natural phenomena which act as cues in the regulation of the body’s circadian rhythms.
This includes light and dark, meals and physical/social activity
Circadian Rhythm
Circadian rhythms, have a period of approximately 24 hours
The word “circadian” originates from Latin, meaning ‘day’
Circadian Dysrhythmia
What we call “jet lag”, is also referred to as desynchronisation
A simple and easy measure of the body’s cycle in relation to wakefulness and sleepiness.
The changes in temperature match up with changes in performance.
People are most alert when temperature is highest and least alert when at its lowest.
Napping
For most individuals, it seems between 10 and 20 minutes of sleep
This involves short sleep involving stages 1-2.
Caffeine
This only postpones and does not remove the effect of sleep loss
Alcohol
While it can make you feel more awake it depresses the CNS
When taken prior to sleep it actually prevents good quality sleep
Sedatives
These can have ‘hangover’ effect making you feel even more tired the next day
Stimulants
E.g. Amphetamines, should be strictly avoided.
Defined as the accumulation of unrelieved stress
Fatigue can be caused by lack of sleep or inadequate rest, environmental stressors, excessive mental or physical activity or disruption of sleep patterns
Fatigue can be acute or chronic. Chronic fatigue can be a serious problem
Any amount of fatigue for a Pilot is dangerous
An increase in errors when trying to complete a task
Decline in performance without recognition
Deterioration of motivation
Time taken to do things increases
Breakdown in scan techniques
Forgetfulness
Slow reaction times
Irritability
Poor judgment and inability to make decisions
Adopt a routine to keep sleep patterns regular.
Avoid coffee and alcohol.
Don’t exercise right before going to sleep.
Use relaxation techniques.
Keep stress levels low.
When changing time zones for more than 24 hours, adopt the local time zone ASAP to avoid jet lag.
Plan sleep in advance, avoid napping if possible.
Physical changes
Vision alters with long-sightedness often developing
Hearing deteriorates
Physical fitness and strength decline
Reflexes and reaction times slow
Older Pilots
Are less impulsive and have fewer accidents where skill is involved
However, information processing can slow down, and the memory can be adversely affected
This mental decline can be prevented to some degree by ‘exercising’ your brain regularly
Dementia
This describes a group of symptoms caused by changes in brain function
Symptoms include repeatedly asking the same question, neglecting personal safety and hygiene and nutrition
Alzheimer’s Disease
This occurs when nerve cell changes in certain parts of the brain result in death of many cells
Symptoms range from mild forgetfulness in the early stages
Progressing to serious impairments in thinking, judgement, and the ability to perform daily activites.
There are several senses used for information acquisition.
The brain processes information to turn it into something we can comprehend; this is called cognition.
Information processing is a continual process of receiving, sorting, deciding upon, filing or discarding data.
Frontal Lobe – cognitive skills, emotions, problem solving, memory, language. The control panel of the personality.
Parietal Lobe – 2 hemispheres, sensory information in relation to body parts, visual information, processing language and mathematics.
Occipital Lobe – connected to the cerebral cortex, visual processing centre.
Temporal Lobe – vision, language, emotion and comprehension.
Cerebellum – sensory system which regulates motor skills, posture, balance, co-ordination and speech.
Attention
The control that you have over what sensed stimuli you choose to process.
Usually being the stimuli that you consider relevant to the task in hand.
Selective Attention
Inputs are sampled and relevant information is drawn out to focus on.
Divided Attention
Attention resources are split between multiple tasks.
The brain can only process one item at a time.
Attention stimulus
Low or high.
If continuous, receptor cells can run into risk of adaptation.
Spatial illusions such as the leans and somatogyral illusions.
Sensory threshold
Stimuli needs to be ‘high’ enough to register.
Sensitivity
Different senses have different levels.
For example, vision being one of the most called upon.
Therefore, the register of caution and warnings are usually associated with colour and movement.
Peripheral / Sensory Memory
Information enters but not all is processed, the attention function allows us to select that which we want, this lasts for a few seconds only
Short Term / Working Memory
Receives information from the sensory memory for further processing, awareness is now present and this lasts for a few minutes.
Long Term Memory
Stored information, lasts forever.
Can be split into semantic (meaning) and episodic (unique to an event).
Motor/Skills Memory
Skills once learned become automatic; they are now in the skills memory, this is part of the long-term memory.
Sensory threshold and sensitivity
This means not all information reaches the sensory memory
Capacity
Limitations of attention means not all information can be attended to
Furthermore, the duration only lasts a few minutes
Anything not transferred to the long-term memory is lost
Perceptual Errors
This can occur and so incorrect information can be stored (reconstruction error)
Interference
This can interrupt the process in the working memory
Associative Interference
Previous learning interferes so the output action is incorrect
Retrieval
It can be difficult to retrieve information from the long-term memory
This is what we view as not being able to remember
Chunking
Grouping items into chunks of information to increase the working memory capacity
Rehearsal
Repetition in order to get information into the long-term memory
Coding
Attaching new information to something you already know
Mnemonics
Helps us retrieve information, e.g. BUMFS checks and IMSAFE
Checklists
This helps in retrieval of information
Mental Workload
The tasks we carry out demand various capabilities such as remembering information and recognizing patterns.
Overloaded
When this demand becomes too high, we refer to it as being overloaded.
Underloaded
If the demand is low, we are underloaded.
Optimal Level
In the arousal/performance curve where does this lie?
As pilots we need to manage potential overload to avoid errors
We can do this by having learned automatic responses to key situations, writing things down, prioritizing, and being well prepared.
We draw a mental picture (mental model) from the information coming into our sensory stores.
This information is compared to our long-term memory.
Different experiences mean people have different perceptions.
However, what we perceive can be biased, confused and misleading.
We combine different information from various sources to draw a mental picture.
Expectation and experience can mean we create a mind-set, and our perception can vary markedly from reality.
Experience:
If we recognize the stimulus the we can more readily absorb it and integrate it into a model of the world around us.
E.g. through experience we know red hot metal will cause pain
E.g. the pattern of position reports
Expectation: can lead us to jump to conclusions
E.g. if an aircraft is on final and did not make a final call, a conclusion can be made (if a thorough lookout is not completed) that the final path is clear
Situational Awareness, Judgement and Decision Making
Having a mental picture of what is happening around you.
Vital for all flight, but particularly while in close proximity to other aircraft (e.g. the circuit) and on critical phases of flight such as take-off, approach and landing.
Good situational awareness will also prevent you getting lost and make you more prepared for any possible emergency.
Pre-flight planning
Briefing intentions
Have a mental picture of traffic in the circuit
When in doubt, ask!
Precise radio calls
Always be prepared for a FLWOP
Always know your position
Beware of mind sets and confirmation bias
Judgement:
The information we choose to process, and the priority we ascribe is a matter of experience and training.
Decision Making:
This is the cognitive process of selecting a course of action from among multiple alternatives.
Knowledge:
Having the information about something.
Skills:
The ability to do something.
Attitudes:
The way you think about, perceive and approach a particular thing.
Deference – deferring to someone else’s opinion
Anti-authority – “rules are for fools!”
Impulsivity – acting before thinking
Invulnerability – it can’t happen to me
Macho – overconfident and out to prove a point
Resignation – it’s out of my control
Get-there-it is – must get there no matter what
Most accidents are a result of a combination of circumstances rather than a single cause.
One poor judgement/error increases the probability of another.
As the errors grows, the alternatives for safe flight decrease.
To avoid an accident, the chain must be broken as soon as the error or poor judgement is recognised.
Ambiguity
Fixation or preoccupation
Confusion
Violating minimums
Departure from SOPs
No-one flying the aircraft
No-one looking out the window
Failure to meet targets
Unresolved discrepancies
Poor communication
Stimuli are received, sorted and perceived and the brain is now in a position to make a decision.
Message is processed, decoded, recognised, understood, classified, acted upon and stored for future use.
If it is a recognised image, there may be previously learnt response in the memory.
Example being aircraft conflict, runway perspective, stall warning sound etc.
Assess
The risk factors for the flight, on the ground.
Take into consideration the pilot, the aircraft, environment, operation.
Flight preparation to improve situational awareness.
Set Limits
Before becoming airborne and stick to them throughout the flight.
Legal minimums vs personal minimums
Set decision points
E.g. Cross country flight in the cruise whether to continue or divert/return.
Maintain situational awareness
Detect a change
Estimate the significance of that change
Choose a safe outcome
Identify all available safe options
Do – put the chosen option into effect
Evaluate the effect of the action
Share information
Analyse information
Develop best solution
Implement your decision
Evaluate the outcome
Fly the aircraft
Diagnose (what is the problem)
Options (hold, divert, immediate landing etc)
Decide (which option)
Act or assign (carry out selected option and assign tasks)
Review (can involve addition of new information, and/or the ongoing result(s) of selected option)
Pilot – health, fatigue, competence
Aircraft – type, fuel state, equipment
Environment – weather, terrain, ATC
Operation – purpose of the flight, urgency
- A superior pilot uses his / her superior judgement to avoid stressful situations which might call for the use of his/her superior skills.
Continuing toward the destination despite adverse conditions
Examples of get-home-itis include:
Racing a thunderstorm to a destination
Failure to go around from an unstabilised approach
Failure to abide by aircraft performance limits
Violating meteorological minimums
Social Psychology
Personality:
This is the pattern of behaviour and ways of thinking that a person uses to adjust to the environment
Extrovert or introvert combined with
Phlegmatic – not easily ruffled
Choleric – hot tempered
Melancholic – sad
Sanguine – cheerful
Operators in the aviation environment should be close partners in terms of “safety” or risk management.
Culture
Safety and situational awareness should be promoted in the work environment.
Radio Communications
This contributes to building the pilot’s and the controller’s situational awareness.
Any ambiguity is minimized in the form of a read back of instructions.
ATC to pilot
Misunderstanding may be prevent by read back
Also providing timely information as well as in plain language
Pilot to pilot
Weather reports
Flight crew reporting
Safety reports
Traffic reports
Engineers to pilot
Defects and operational symptoms to be wary of
Operating requirement of aircraft released for service, e.g. running a new engine in with the use of straight mineral oil
Conducting flight checks
Human error is inevitable and generally occurs inadvertently, comparatively, rarely and randomly.
Accidents rarely have a single casual factor.
One of a pilot’s principal jobs is to recover from mistakes or failures of elements in the system, including his/her own.
The industry’s aim must be to minimize errors and the operational consequences when errors do occur.
Those threats and errors occurring in direct contact with the system. They take the form of slips, lapses, fumbles, mistakes and procedural violations.
Active failures have a direct and usually short-lived impact on the system.
These arise from decisions made by designers, builders, procedure writers, and top-level management.
They can cause error provoking conditions and/or long-lasting holes or weaknesses in the system’s defenses.
E.g. time pressure, understaffing, inadequate equipment, unworkable procedures, unreliable alarm systems, construction deficiencies.
Latent conditions can lie dormant for years until combined with active failures to trigger an accident.
Every step in a process has the potential for failure, to varying degrees.

Reason hypothesizes that most accidents can be traced to one or more of four levels of failure, for example;
Organisational influences
Unsafe supervision
Preconditions for unsafe acts
Unsafe acts themselves
Ensure open communication
Promote teamwork
Reinforce desired behaviours
Intuition – “Gut feeling”
Assess personal approach and capabilities
Attitude – assertive, conservative, diligent
Review task demands, equipment, barriers, personal and team skill
Mitigate
The undesirable state of the aircraft is resolved. Recovery has occurred and safe flight continues.
Exacerbate
The severity of the state and level of risk is further increased. This will lead to additional errors of an incident/accident.
Failure to Respond
Nothing is done to recover to safe flight. Again, this results in additional errors or an incident/accident.

Documents and Procedures
Flight deck documentation includes manuals, checklists, operational data cards, flight operations bulletins, maps, charts, approach plates and that’s just the beginning!
Checklists: Ensures that all required actions are performed without omission and in an orderly manner. Redundancy as human memory has limitation and failures.
Elements of an effective checklist:
Easily found
Easily read day and night
Concise
Clear and unambiguous
Not add to pilot workload
Normal:
Challenge and response
Read and do
Emergency:
Includes immediate actions to be memorized
As well as expanded step by step sections
Expanded:
A supplement to the above two
Not used in flight but for training or to review procedures
Most accidents that occur due to checklist misuse occur on the takeoff, approach and landing phases.
One human characteristic that we need to guard against when using checklist is to not see what we want to see but to see what really exists.
For example, selecting the ‘gear down?’
Check the possible indications such as light indications, speed and attitude change.
On occasions pilots automatically verbalise “three greens” when in fact it is not the case.
Understand the reason for the checklist and the items on it.
Careful verification of checklist items.
Routine use encouraged to avoid complacency.

Complacency:
This is caused by the very things that should prevent accidents.
Factors like experience, training and knowledge contribute to complacency.
Complacency makes crews:
Skip hurriedly through checklists
Failure to monitor instruments closely or to utilize Nav Aids
Use shortcuts, rely on judgement and malpractices
Outcome of complacency:
These effects can mean the difference between safe and unsafe flight.

A person operating an aircraft carrying passengers must ensure that each person has been briefed appropriately, with a number of items that are mandatory to be briefed:
Conditions under which smoking is prohibited
Stowage of passenger service equipment
Occupation of seats and wearing of restraints
Location and means for opening the passenger entry doors and exits
Procedures in the case of an emergency landing
Use of portable electronic devices
These briefing points can usually be summed up in a spoken safety brief or more commonly a safety video.
Air NZ Safety Video - Bear Grylls
There are 5 Basic Principles of Survival in importance of priority:
1. The Will to Survive – “I will survive!”
2. Location – Maximise the chances of being found, activate ELT, higher ground away from flood risk areas and hazards.
3. Shelter – Protection from harsh effects of the weather.
4. Water – the body can withstand only for a few days without water.
5. Food – the body can withstand 1-2 weeks without food.

A condition in which an organism’s temperature drops below that required for normal metabolism and bodily functions.
When your body temperature drop, your heart, nervous system and other organs can’t work normally.
Left untreated, hypothermia can eventually lead to a complete failure of your heart and respiratory system and eventually to death.
Normal body temperature is around 37˚C.
Hypothermia occurs as your body temperature falls below 35˚C.
Hypothermia Video
Initial hunger and nausea will give way to apathy as the core body temperature drops.
The next symptoms to develop are confusion, lethargy, slurred speech, loss of consciousness and coma.
Often the affect person will lie down, fall asleep and die.
Some individuals will paradoxically remove their clothes just before this occurs, a phenomena called paradoxical undressing.
Prevention:
Appropriate clothing – cotton is not good as it hold water
20-40% heat loss is through the head
Get dry, for the same temperature, being wet is much worse than dry
Alcohol consumption prior increases the risk
Get dry, get shelter and gradually warm.
Portable tents onsite treatment.
Do not rub the skin.
Use blankets and body heat to warm.
The core of the body must be warmed first.
Drink sweet, warm liquids.
Get to hospital.
A hypothermic person is not dead until they are warm and dead.
